messages.content: I want to develop a multimodal predictor that is robust to label-dependent modality missingness shifts without sacrificing accuracy when all modalities are observed. How should I state the goal precisely?

The goal has two linked requirements. Under unseen label-dependent missingness, reduce worst-pattern error by 10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline. When all modalities are observed, retain accuracy within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline. Both requirements matter: robustness under missingness should not come at the expense of complete-modality performance.
What does “label-dependent modality missingness” mean here?

It means which modalities are available can depend on the label, rather than missingness being unrelated to what the predictor is trying to predict. The goal concerns shifts of that kind that are unseen. It does not specify a particular missingness mechanism, set of modalities, or direction in which availability changes.
And what is a missingness pattern?

A missingness pattern identifies which modalities are observed and which are missing. “Worst-pattern error” focuses on the pattern with the highest error among the patterns being evaluated, rather than an average that could conceal poor performance for one pattern. The goal does not specify the precise collection of patterns used for that comparison.
So the 10% target applies to that worst-pattern error, not to average accuracy?

Yes. The stated target is a 10% relative reduction in worst-pattern error under unseen label-dependent missingness. It does not, by itself, set an average-accuracy target for those missingness conditions.
Can you clarify “relative to the strongest unimodal baseline”?

The comparator is the strongest unimodal baseline, not an arbitrary or weaker unimodal predictor. The requested improvement is measured against that baseline’s worst-pattern error under the relevant unseen label-dependent missingness evaluation. The statement does not say which modality supplies that baseline or give its numerical error.
I want to be sure I am not confusing a relative error reduction with a percentage-point difference.

For the missingness requirement, “10% relative” means the target worst-pattern error is at most 90% of the strongest unimodal baseline’s worst-pattern error. It does not mean subtracting 10 percentage points from that error. The complete-modality requirement uses a different kind of comparison: an accuracy difference of one percentage point.
Why keep the complete-modality requirement separate?

Because it guards a distinct part of the goal. Reducing error when modalities are missing would not, on its own, establish that the predictor remains accurate when every modality is present. The complete-modality requirement makes that condition explicit by comparing accuracy with an equally trained complete-modality baseline.
What exactly is the allowed complete-modality gap?

The stated criterion is to retain complete-modality accuracy within one percentage point of the equally trained complete-modality baseline. In particular, a loss of more than one percentage point would not satisfy that requirement. No baseline accuracy value is supplied, so the criterion remains a comparison rather than a numerical accuracy target.
Does “equally trained” tell us how either predictor must be built?

No particular architecture or training method is specified. “Equally trained” qualifies the complete-modality baseline used for the accuracy comparison; it should not be expanded into an unstated implementation choice or a detailed training protocol.
Is the goal claiming the predictor already achieves either threshold?

No. It describes what the predictor is intended to achieve. There are no results here establishing the 10% relative worst-pattern error reduction or the one-percentage-point complete-modality accuracy condition.
Suppose the predictor performs well with all modalities present but fails on one missingness pattern. Would that meet the goal?

Not if that pattern makes its worst-pattern error miss the required 10% relative reduction against the strongest unimodal baseline under the relevant unseen label-dependent missingness. Meeting the complete-modality accuracy requirement alone is insufficient; the two stated requirements must be considered together.
And if it reaches the missingness target but loses too much complete-modality accuracy?

That would likewise fall short of the stated goal if its complete-modality accuracy is more than one percentage point below the equally trained complete-modality baseline. The robustness target does not replace the accuracy-retention target.
Does “unseen” mean I should describe a particular new missingness pattern?

Not from this goal alone. “Unseen” identifies the intended shift condition for the robustness requirement, but no particular pattern or shift is named. You can preserve that condition without asserting how the unseen shift is generated or which modalities it affects.
Could you give me a compact formulation that keeps the two comparisons distinct?

Develop a multimodal predictor robust to unseen label-dependent modality missingness shifts, reducing worst-pattern error by 10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline while keeping accuracy when all modalities are observed within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline.
What should I be careful not to imply when discussing it?

Avoid implying that an average over missingness patterns can substitute for worst-pattern error, that the 10% figure is a percentage-point reduction, or that complete-modality accuracy is compared with the unimodal baseline. Also avoid presenting a particular model design, evaluation outcome, or missingness mechanism as already specified.
Then the central tension is robustness to the unseen label-dependent shift while preserving performance with full observations?

Exactly. The goal asks for both: a specified relative improvement in the worst missingness-pattern error against the strongest unimodal baseline, and complete-modality accuracy within one percentage point of its equally trained complete-modality comparator. Neither condition should be treated as a substitute for the other.

For that goal, I propose training class-balanced subset fusion experts under adversarial label-conditioned dropout, while preserving a separately supervised complete-modality branch. Can you unpack the proposal without treating it as a proven solution?

The proposal has two complementary parts. Class-balanced subset fusion experts would be trained to make use of available modality subsets, with adversarial label-conditioned dropout supplying challenging training-time missingness. Separately, a complete-modality branch would retain its own supervision for the case in which all modalities are observed. This is a proposed training approach, not evidence that either performance requirement has been met.
What do “subset fusion experts” contribute conceptually?

They focus the predictor on making use of the modalities that remain available, rather than assuming that every modality is always present. “Fusion” indicates that the experts are intended to combine information from available modalities. The proposal does not specify how many experts there are, which subsets each covers, or how their outputs are selected or combined.
Why specify that those experts are class-balanced?

The class-balanced qualification says their training should not be dominated by particular classes. That matters conceptually when training for label-dependent missingness: an expert should not simply have its learning shaped by whichever classes happen to receive the most emphasis. The proposal does not prescribe a balancing formula or claim that class balance alone ensures robustness.
Is class balancing the same as making every missingness pattern equally common?

No. Class balance concerns representation or emphasis across labels. Balance across missingness patterns would be a different property. Nothing in the proposal specifies equal frequency for every pattern, so the two should not be conflated.
How should I read “label-conditioned dropout” in this setting?

It means that, during training, the choice of which modalities to drop can depend on the label. This lets the training setup address missingness related to the prediction target, rather than considering only dropout independent of the label. The proposal does not specify the exact label-to-dropout relationship or any particular dropout probabilities.
And what does the adversarial part add?

“Adversarial” indicates that dropout is intended to present challenging missing-modality conditions to the training process, rather than merely following an unspecified fixed random choice. The proposal does not define the adversary, its objective, or its constraints. It also does not claim that the resulting training conditions cover every unseen label-dependent shift.
So I should not describe a particular worst-case dropout rule as if it were already chosen?

Correct. You can say the proposal calls for adversarial label-conditioned dropout, but a specific rule for selecting dropped modalities would add a design choice that is not stated. Likewise, the proposal does not identify any particular modality as more likely to be dropped for any class.
Does conditioning dropout on labels imply the predictor is given the true label when it makes predictions?

No such inference follows from the proposal. Label-conditioned dropout describes a training-time way to produce missingness. It does not specify that a true label is supplied to the predictor at prediction time, nor does it define the predictor’s inference procedure.
What is the purpose of preserving a separately supervised complete-modality branch?

It keeps the all-modalities-observed case explicitly represented in training, with its own supervision, while the subset experts are trained for missing-modality conditions. Conceptually, that responds to the part of the goal requiring complete-modality accuracy to remain close to an equally trained complete-modality baseline. Preserving that branch is an approach to protecting accuracy, not a guarantee that the one-percentage-point condition will hold.
Does “separately supervised” mean the complete-modality branch cannot share anything with the subset experts?

Not necessarily. The phrase establishes distinct supervision for the complete-modality branch; it does not, on its own, settle whether parameters, representations, or other components are shared. The architectural boundary is not specified.
Should I say the complete-modality branch replaces the subset experts whenever all modalities are available?

The proposal preserves a branch for the complete-modality case, but it does not specify a routing or output-selection rule. Saying that it necessarily replaces the experts would go beyond what is stated. You can describe its separately supervised role without committing to how predictions are dispatched.
How do the two parts of the proposal relate to the two performance requirements?

The subset experts and adversarial label-conditioned dropout are directed at robustness when availability of modalities shifts in a label-dependent way. The separately supervised complete-modality branch is directed at retaining accuracy when all modalities are observed. The intended alignment is clear, but the proposal alone does not establish the required 10% relative reduction in worst-pattern error or the one-percentage-point complete-modality accuracy bound.
Is it fair to say that dropout is intended to make training harder in a relevant way, rather than to reproduce the exact unseen shift?

Yes, as a conceptual reading. Adversarial label-conditioned dropout is proposed as challenging training exposure relevant to label-dependent missingness. There is no specified unseen shift to reproduce exactly, and no claim that the training dropout matches any particular future missingness process.
Could class balance and adversarial dropout pull in different directions?

They address different aspects of training, so their interaction is a legitimate consideration. Class balance concerns emphasis across labels; adversarial label-conditioned dropout concerns challenging patterns of modality removal that can depend on labels. The proposal states that they are to be used together, but it does not define how any competing pressures are resolved or report what happens when they interact.
I also want to avoid implying that the complete-modality branch has already protected accuracy. What wording works?

You could say: “Preserve a separately supervised complete-modality branch to address the risk of losing accuracy when all modalities are observed.” That states its intended role without claiming a measured benefit or saying the accuracy requirement has already been satisfied.
Can the subset experts be described as solving unseen label-dependent missingness?

Not as an established fact. They are proposed as a way to train for missing-modality prediction under challenging, label-conditioned dropout. Whether they achieve the required worst-pattern error improvement under unseen label-dependent missingness remains an outcome to be determined, not a property established by the proposal.
Give me one faithful sentence that includes the whole proposed approach.

Train class-balanced subset fusion experts under adversarial label-conditioned dropout to address missing-modality robustness, while retaining a separately supervised complete-modality branch for the all-modalities-observed case.
That sentence should still be read as a proposal, with neither comparison target assumed achieved, right?

Right. It names the proposed training structure and its intended roles. It does not assert a 10% relative reduction in worst-pattern error against the strongest unimodal baseline under unseen label-dependent missingness, or complete-modality accuracy within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline.
How can the subset experts avoid exploiting label-correlated missingness masks if those correlations reverse at deployment?

The key distinction is between using a mask to know which modalities are available and using it as a shortcut for predicting the label. An expert needs the first use to handle a subset of modalities. The concern is the second: if a mask tends to accompany one label during training, the expert might learn that association instead of relying on evidence in the observed modalities. A reversal at deployment could then make the association misleading.
So a subset expert can respond to the mask without treating the mask itself as evidence of the label?

Conceptually, yes. The mask can identify the prediction situation—what information is available—without being treated as a dependable label cue. That is the distinction the question asks how to maintain. The proposal does not yet specify a mechanism that enforces it.
Why is this especially relevant to adversarial label-conditioned dropout?

Because label-conditioned dropout allows modality availability during training to depend on the label. That makes it important to ask whether an expert is learning to predict from the remaining modality content or from an association between labels and availability. Calling the dropout adversarial does not, by itself, rule out the latter.
Would class-balancing the experts resolve the problem?

Not necessarily. Class balance addresses how much emphasis different labels receive, but it does not automatically remove an association between a particular mask and a label. It is possible in principle for labels to be balanced overall while their frequencies still differ across masks. The question is whether the experts depend on those mask–label associations.
Can you illustrate the failure mode without assuming a particular dataset or set of modalities?

Imagine that, during training, one availability pattern appears more often with one label than another. A predictor that leans on that association could appear effective even when the observed modality content provides little support for its guess. If the association reverses at deployment, the same shortcut points in the wrong direction. This is only an illustration of the concern, not a claim that it has happened here.
Is simply hiding the mask from an expert the answer?

Not automatically. The expert still has to deal with whichever modalities are present, so availability matters to how it uses its inputs. The aim is not necessarily to make the expert unaware of missingness; it is to avoid making the training-time relationship between missingness and labels the basis for its label prediction. No specific way of achieving that has been selected in the stated proposal.
What would it mean, at a conceptual level, for an expert to rely on the observed modalities instead?

It would mean that the expert’s prediction is supported by information in the modalities it actually receives, while the mask tells it the limits of that information. The difficult part is distinguishing that behavior from a prediction that happens to correlate with the right label because of the training-time mask distribution. The current question raises that distinction without asserting that the experts already satisfy it.
Could a model do both—use observed content and still pick up the shortcut?

Yes. These are not mutually exclusive behaviors. An expert could use useful observed information and also lean on a mask–label correlation. That is why some ability to predict under a training distribution would not, on its own, settle whether the expert remains reliable when that correlation reverses.
Does the reversal mean the available modalities themselves have changed meaning?

The question does not say that. It specifically concerns a reversal of the correlation between missingness masks and labels at deployment. That is enough to threaten a mask-based shortcut; it does not require assuming a change in the meaning of the observed modality content.
How should I phrase the design principle without claiming an implementation?

You could say: “Train subset experts to use missingness masks to identify available inputs, without depending on the training-time association between those masks and labels for prediction.” That expresses the desired distinction. It does not claim that the proposed class balance or adversarial dropout already guarantees it.
Does adversarial dropout necessarily expose the experts to a reversal of the mask–label correlation?

No. “Adversarial label-conditioned dropout” says that challenging dropout can depend on labels, but it does not specify which associations appear during training or whether a reversal is included. We should not infer coverage of the deployment reversal from that phrase alone.
Then what is still open in the question?

What remains open is how to prevent the experts from using an unstable mask–label association while still letting them handle different available modality subsets. It is also open whether the proposed training approach succeeds when the deployment association reverses. Neither an enforcement mechanism nor an outcome is specified here.
Would it be accurate to say the risk is distribution shift rather than just ordinary missing inputs?

Yes, with a precise qualification: the risk in this question is a shift in how missingness masks relate to labels. The experts may be prepared to receive missing inputs yet still be vulnerable if their predictions rely on a mask–label relationship that changes. Handling a subset and being robust to a reversal of its label correlation are distinct concerns.
How does this concern relate to the worst-pattern error requirement?

If predictions for a particular availability pattern depend heavily on a reversed mask–label correlation, that pattern could have high error. The stated goal evaluates worst-pattern error under unseen label-dependent missingness, so the shortcut concern is relevant to it. The question does not establish that such a failure occurs or that addressing it would achieve the required 10% relative reduction against the strongest unimodal baseline.
Does the separately supervised complete-modality branch remove this concern for the subset experts?

No such conclusion follows. That branch addresses the case where all modalities are observed and has its own supervision. The present question is about how subset experts behave when a label-correlated missingness mask becomes misleading. Preserving the complete-modality branch does not, by itself, answer that question.
Can I describe the mask as potentially useful but not necessarily trustworthy?

Yes. It is useful as a description of availability: it tells the predictor what it can draw on. Its training-time correlation with a label is not necessarily trustworthy when the correlation may reverse at deployment. Keeping those two meanings separate captures the issue.
And we should leave the actual way to maintain that separation unresolved for now?

Yes. The precise open question is how subset experts can use masks to accommodate missing modalities without exploiting label correlations in those masks that may reverse at deployment. The proposal names class-balanced experts and adversarial label-conditioned dropout, but it does not specify or demonstrate a solution to that shortcut risk.

Here is a hypothesis about the mask-shortcut concern: class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings will cut reversed-mask worst-pattern error by at least 10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline. Can we state that carefully?

Yes. The hypothesis is that class-balanced subset experts trained without mask embeddings will achieve a ≥10% relative reduction in worst-pattern error when mask–label correlations reverse, compared with the strongest unimodal baseline. It is a prediction about performance, not an observed result or a guarantee that omitting mask embeddings prevents every use of missingness information.
What work is “without mask embeddings” doing in that hypothesis?

It identifies a specific restriction: the subset experts would not receive learned embeddings of the missingness masks as an explicit input representation. The motivation is the concern that such a representation could make a training-time mask–label association easy to exploit. The hypothesis does not establish that removing it is sufficient to avoid that shortcut.
Does that mean the experts are unaware of which modalities are available?

Not necessarily. A subset expert must still operate on the modalities that are available to it. Omitting mask embeddings is narrower than asserting that availability can never be inferred or used in any way. The proposed prediction concerns the resulting worst-pattern error under reversed-mask conditions, not complete ignorance of missingness.
Why keep “class-balanced” in the statement instead of attributing everything to the lack of mask embeddings?

Because the hypothesis is about class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings as a combination. It does not isolate the effect of class balance from the effect of omitting mask embeddings, or claim that either feature alone produces the predicted reduction.
What exactly is reversing in “reversed-mask”?

The relevant reversal is in the correlation between missingness masks and labels at deployment. A mask associated with labels one way during training may be associated with them differently when deployed. The term does not, by itself, assert that the meanings of the observed modalities reverse.
And “worst-pattern error” still refers to the most difficult availability pattern in the evaluation?

It refers to the highest error across the missingness patterns being evaluated under the reversed-mask condition. The claim concerns that worst-pattern value, not merely an overall average. The hypothesis does not specify the set of patterns or their individual error values.
Could you translate the 10% comparison into a simple mathematical reading?

If the strongest unimodal baseline’s reversed-mask worst-pattern error is B, the hypothesized threshold for the class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings is at most 0.90 × B. That expresses a reduction of at least 10% relative to the baseline’s error, rather than a subtraction of 10 percentage points.
Does “strongest unimodal baseline” mean we can pick whichever one makes the comparison easiest?

No. The wording calls for comparison with the strongest unimodal baseline, not a conveniently weaker one. It does not identify which unimodal predictor is strongest or supply its error, so those details should not be assumed.
Is this hypothesis a full claim about the original multimodal goal?

No. It makes a specific predicted comparison for reversed-mask worst-pattern error. It does not claim an outcome for every kind of unseen label-dependent missingness shift, and it says nothing about whether complete-modality accuracy remains within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline.
The larger proposal also mentioned adversarial label-conditioned dropout. Should I put that in this hypothesis?

The hypothesis as stated names class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings and predicts a reversed-mask worst-pattern error reduction. It does not specify dropout in the claim itself. You can identify the experts as part of the broader proposed approach, but adding a particular dropout condition to this hypothesis would change what it explicitly says.
Is the reason for omitting mask embeddings that the experts otherwise definitely memorize the mask–label correlation?

That would be too strong. The concern is that label-correlated masks can offer a shortcut, and omitting mask embeddings is a hypothesized way to limit reliance on an explicit mask representation. Neither inevitable memorization with embeddings nor reliable protection without them is established by this hypothesis.
Could they still pick up information about the missingness pattern indirectly?

In principle, yes. Which modalities are present can be apparent from what an expert receives, even without a mask embedding. That possibility is why the restriction should not be paraphrased as ‘the experts cannot exploit missingness.’ The predicted ≥10% relative error reduction remains a hypothesis to be assessed.
Then is this really answering the earlier question about avoiding mask shortcuts?

It offers a candidate answer in the form of a testable performance hypothesis: class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings are predicted to do better on reversed-mask worst-pattern error than the strongest unimodal baseline by at least 10% relatively. It does not prove that the experts avoid all shortcuts or specify exactly what they rely on when predicting.
Could the threshold be met even if the experts still use some mask information?

Yes, conceptually. The threshold is stated in terms of worst-pattern error under reversal, not a direct claim that the experts use no mask-related information. Observing the required relative error reduction would not, by itself, establish that their predictions never depend on availability cues.
Conversely, would omitting mask embeddings itself count as meeting the hypothesis?

No. Omitting mask embeddings describes the proposed experts; the hypothesis also predicts a measurable outcome: reversed-mask worst-pattern error at least 10% lower, relatively, than that of the strongest unimodal baseline. The design description alone cannot establish the error comparison.
If someone reports an improvement in average error under reversal, can I treat that as confirmation?

Not on its own. The prediction is specifically about worst-pattern error. An improvement in average error might coexist with a missingness pattern whose error remains too high to satisfy the hypothesized worst-pattern comparison.
And an absolute drop of 10 percentage points would not be the precise criterion either?

Correct. The criterion is a reduction of at least 10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline’s reversed-mask worst-pattern error. A percentage-point statement uses a different scale; whether any particular absolute drop satisfies the relative threshold would depend on the baseline’s error.
What level of certainty should the wording convey?

Use explicit hypothesis language, such as ‘We hypothesize that’ or ‘The prediction is that.’ The phrase ‘will cut’ states the predicted outcome, but should not be presented as a completed finding. No performance measurement is provided here.
Can you write a concise version without losing the condition or comparator?
We hypothesize that class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings will reduce worst-pattern error under reversed mask–label correlations by ≥10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline.
Should I say this guarantees accuracy when all modalities are present because the broader proposal preserves a separate branch?

No. This hypothesis does not predict complete-modality accuracy. The separately supervised complete-modality branch is part of the broader proposal, but its presence does not establish that the accuracy difference from an equally trained complete-modality baseline stays within one percentage point.
So the main caution is to keep the proposed design, the predicted reversed-mask improvement, and an actual result distinct?

Exactly. ‘Class-balanced subset experts without mask embeddings’ identifies the proposed experts; ‘≥10% relative reduction in reversed-mask worst-pattern error versus the strongest unimodal baseline’ is the prediction. Neither the design’s effectiveness nor that measured reduction is established by the hypothesis itself.

I want to turn the mask-shortcut concern into a plan: train mask-blind, class-balanced subset experts; then test reversed label-dependent dropout and compare worst-pattern error and complete-modality accuracy against baselines. Can you unpack what that commits us to?

It commits to training subset experts that are class-balanced and mask-blind, then evaluating them under reversed label-dependent dropout. The planned comparisons cover two outcomes: worst-pattern error under the missingness test and accuracy when all modalities are observed. This is a plan for training and comparison, not a report that the experts avoid mask shortcuts or meet either performance target.
What should “mask-blind” mean in that wording?

It expresses the intended restriction against using the missingness mask itself as an explicit label-predictive input. It should not be read as a guarantee that an expert has no indication of which modalities it received: availability may be apparent from the inputs it can process. The plan does not specify an architecture or a particular way to enforce mask blindness.
Is that the same as saying the experts will be unable to exploit missingness?

No. Even without an explicit mask input, an expert might indirectly distinguish availability patterns. The plan addresses the shortcut concern by proposing mask-blind experts and a test under reversed label-dependent dropout; it does not establish that all dependence on missingness has been eliminated.
Why retain class balance in the training part?

Class balance is an explicit property of the experts to be trained. It concerns the emphasis given to different labels. It is not equivalent to making every missingness pattern equally frequent, and it does not by itself establish that the experts will ignore correlations between patterns and labels.
Does the plan specify how class balance is achieved?
No. It calls for class-balanced subset experts without choosing a balancing procedure. Adding a particular sampling, weighting, or optimization rule would make the plan more specific than stated.
Where does reversed label-dependent dropout enter: training or testing?

In this plan, it is explicitly the test condition. The training instruction is to train mask-blind, class-balanced subset experts. The plan does not specify that the reversed dropout used for testing is also used during training.
What does the reversal test probe?

It probes performance when the relationship between missingness and labels reverses. If predictions lean on the training-time association between a mask and a label, that association may become misleading under the test condition. The test can reveal a performance problem under reversal, though the plan does not claim in advance what the result will be.
Should I describe the test as proving that the experts rely only on observed modality content?

No. The planned test compares predictive performance under reversed label-dependent dropout. Performance under that condition is relevant to the shortcut concern, but an error comparison alone would not prove that the experts rely exclusively on observed modality content or identify every cue they use.
Why compare worst-pattern error rather than only an aggregate error?

Worst-pattern error keeps attention on the availability pattern with the highest error among those evaluated. An aggregate could look favorable while one pattern remains difficult. The plan specifically names worst-pattern error, so an aggregate result alone would not answer that part of the planned comparison.
Which baseline matters for that worst-pattern comparison?

For the stated robustness goal, the comparator is the strongest unimodal baseline. The plan says to compare against baselines; using that comparator makes the worst-pattern comparison relevant to the goal’s requirement of a 10% relative error reduction under unseen label-dependent missingness. The plan does not name the strongest unimodal predictor or give its error.
Does the reversed-dropout test automatically cover every unseen label-dependent missingness shift?

No. Reversed label-dependent dropout is the test condition named in this plan. Results under it would speak to that condition; they should not automatically be generalized to every possible unseen label-dependent missingness shift.
What is the separate role of complete-modality accuracy in the comparisons?

It checks performance when all modalities are observed, rather than when a subset is missing. The broader goal is to retain that accuracy within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline. Including it in the plan prevents the missingness comparison from being the only measure considered.
Is the complete-modality comparison made against the strongest unimodal baseline too?

No. The two goal-level comparators are distinct: worst-pattern error is compared with the strongest unimodal baseline, while complete-modality accuracy is compared with an equally trained complete-modality baseline. The plan calls for both kinds of comparison, not one shared baseline for both outcomes.
Does this plan specify how a complete-modality prediction is produced?

It specifies that complete-modality accuracy will be compared, but not the precise prediction route or architecture used when all modalities are present. The separately supervised complete-modality branch belongs to the proposed approach already discussed; this plan does not add details about how its output would interact with the subset experts.
Would a good reversed-dropout result make the complete-modality comparison unnecessary?

No. Worst-pattern error under reversed missingness and accuracy with all modalities observed address different conditions. The plan includes both comparisons because performance on one does not establish performance on the other.
And if complete-modality accuracy is strong, could I skip worst-pattern error?

Not while carrying out this plan. Strong complete-modality accuracy would not show how the experts perform on the hardest missingness pattern under reversed label-dependent dropout. The planned worst-pattern comparison remains a separate check.
Should the plan say the reversal is something we expect to encounter at deployment?

The shortcut question concerns what happens if mask–label correlations reverse at deployment, and the plan tests a reversed label-dependent dropout condition. It does not establish that any particular deployment setting will exhibit that reversal. It is safer to describe reversal as the condition being tested.
Can we call the training step a solution to the shortcut problem?

Not yet. Mask-blind, class-balanced subset experts are the proposed training choice. Testing under reversal and comparing errors are how the plan examines the concern. Without results, the plan cannot establish that the shortcut problem has been solved.
What if someone says that omitting an explicit mask makes the test redundant?

That would assume more than mask blindness guarantees. Experts may still encounter different available subsets, and the effect of reversed label-dependent missingness on their predictions remains an empirical question. The test is therefore meaningful even if no explicit mask representation is supplied.
Does the plan require us to infer why an expert made each prediction?

No. It names training mask-blind, class-balanced subset experts, testing reversed label-dependent dropout, and comparing two performance measures against baselines. It does not specify an additional analysis of individual predictions or a method for attributing their causes.
What conclusion would be premature before those comparisons are available?

It would be premature to say that the experts reduce reversed-mask worst-pattern error by at least 10% relative to the strongest unimodal baseline, or that complete-modality accuracy is within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline. Both are comparison targets, not outcomes supplied by the plan.
Can you give me a single-sentence version of the plan that preserves the training–testing distinction?
Train mask-blind, class-balanced subset experts, then test them under reversed label-dependent dropout and compare worst-pattern error and complete-modality accuracy with their respective baselines.
And the reason for testing the reversal is the possibility that availability patterns became label shortcuts?

Yes. The reversal test is directed at the concern that a predictor might rely on a training-time association between missingness masks and labels that becomes misleading when that association reverses. The planned comparisons will assess performance under that condition; they do not, by themselves, presuppose either success or failure.

For the activity, train CMU-MOSEI class-balanced, mask-blind subset experts with a separately supervised full-input branch, then compare reversed-mask error and complete-input accuracy against baselines. What does that specify?

It specifies CMU-MOSEI as the setting, class-balanced and mask-blind subset experts as the experts to train, and a full-input branch that receives separate supervision. It also specifies two comparisons: error under reversed mask–label correlations and accuracy when the complete input is available. The activity does not report training results or either comparison’s outcome.
Does naming CMU-MOSEI tell us which particular modalities or subsets the experts use?

Not in this activity. It names CMU-MOSEI, but it does not enumerate the subsets assigned to experts or prescribe how many experts to train. Those details should not be filled in as though they were stated.
What is an expert expected to do if it is mask-blind but receives only a subset of the input?

It is expected to make a prediction from the modalities available to that expert. Mask-blindness means the missingness mask is not supplied as an explicit label-predictive representation; it does not mean the expert somehow receives modalities that are absent or cannot distinguish what input it has been given. The activity does not specify the mechanism used to handle each subset.
Could I equate mask-blindness here with the earlier idea of omitting mask embeddings?

That is a reasonable way to express the intended restriction on an explicit mask representation. Keep the claim narrow, though: omitting mask embeddings does not prove that an expert cannot infer an availability pattern from its inputs or exploit it indirectly.
What does class-balanced add to the training instruction?

It says the subset experts’ training should balance emphasis across classes. It does not specify how that balance is achieved, and it does not mean every missingness pattern has to appear equally often. Both qualifications—class-balanced and mask-blind—apply to the subset experts named in the activity.
Is the separately supervised full-input branch another subset expert?

The activity distinguishes it from the subset experts: it is a branch for the complete input, with separate supervision. That distinction does not settle whether any internal components are shared or how a prediction is selected when all inputs are present.
Why keep that branch in the same activity as the subset experts?

It keeps the all-inputs-available case in view while training experts for incomplete inputs.
