Logits are the model’s output scores before they are converted into a final prediction or normalized probabilities. Here, they are the quantities the plan proposes to align. Saying “logits” is more specific than saying only that the subset experts and teacher should behave similarly, but the plan does not specify an alignment loss or how close the scores must become.
What does “paired subset logits” mean without assuming an elaborate pairing scheme?

It indicates that subset outputs are paired with corresponding teacher outputs for alignment, rather than compared as unrelated collections of scores. The plan does not specify which subsets are paired, how many pairs are formed, or a procedure for constructing them.
Is the full-input teacher another name for the subset experts?

No. The wording distinguishes logits from subset inputs from a teacher that uses the full input. The teacher supplies the reference for alignment; the subset experts are the predictors whose logits are to be aligned. The plan does not specify their architectures or whether they share components.
What exactly is frozen about the teacher?

The teacher is held fixed during the proposed alignment, rather than being changed by that alignment step. “Frozen” does not tell us how it was trained, what accuracy it has, or whether any other part of the system is fixed.
Does using a full-input teacher imply that full inputs will be available when the subset experts are deployed?

No. The teacher is named as a reference in the alignment step. The plan does not say that the full input or the teacher’s output is available when a subset expert later has to predict from missing modalities.
Are we requiring each subset expert to produce exactly the same logits as the teacher?

The plan calls for aligning logits, but it gives no exact-equality requirement or tolerance. Subset inputs may contain less information than the full input, so describing the plan as guaranteeing identical scores would go beyond its wording.
Could I specify a particular alignment loss when I restate this plan?

That would add an implementation choice. A faithful restatement can say that paired subset logits will be aligned to a frozen full-input teacher, while leaving the loss function and optimization details unspecified.
Does alignment itself demonstrate that the teacher is always correct?

No. The teacher provides a fixed full-input reference, but the plan gives no result about its accuracy or the correctness of any individual output. Aligning to its logits is a proposed approach, not proof that its predictions are error-free.
How does this plan relate conceptually to the possibility of within-class modality-feature selection?

The measurement part asks whether feature distributions differ within classes. The alignment part proposes using a fixed full-input reference for corresponding subset outputs. Together, those steps investigate and respond to the concern that the information seen under a subset may differ in ways not captured by class alone. That is the plan’s rationale, not a finding that such selection occurs or that alignment remedies it.
Could alignment improve reversal performance even if the shift measurement finds little difference?

The plan does not rule that out. The shift measurement and the evaluation are separate observations. An error change would not, by itself, prove that class-conditional feature shift was the reason for it, just as a shift measurement would not guarantee an error change.
What is being evaluated under “reversals”?

The plan calls for evaluating predictive performance when the missingness relationship is reversed. It does not specify the reversal definitions, their number, or the numerical outcome here. That evaluation is distinct from measuring feature shift and from aligning the logits.
Should I assume the same error on every reversal once the logits are aligned?
No. Alignment is a proposed training step, not a guarantee of uniform performance. The plan specifically calls for evaluation under reversals, so their results remain open.
Why also evaluate complete-input accuracy?

Because performance when all inputs are present is a separate concern from performance under reversed missingness. Checking complete-input accuracy allows that condition to be assessed rather than assuming an alignment strategy for subsets leaves it unchanged. The plan reports no complete-input accuracy value.
Is complete-input accuracy automatically the teacher’s accuracy?

The plan does not say so. It identifies a frozen full-input teacher for alignment and separately calls for evaluating complete-input accuracy. It does not specify which output is used for that accuracy calculation or state that the two must coincide.
Can I claim that freezing the teacher protects complete-input accuracy?

Not from this plan alone. Freezing means the teacher is not updated during alignment. It does not establish how complete-input predictions are made or what their measured accuracy will be; that is why complete-input accuracy remains an evaluation item.
Does this plan itself commit to a 25.2% worst-pattern error result?

No. It describes measuring, aligning, and evaluating. The proposed ≤25.2% worst-pattern error is a performance hypothesis for counterfactual subset alignment, not a result supplied by this plan. No reversal error is reported here.
If an evaluation found an error at exactly 25.2%, how should I keep the comparison precise?

The associated ≤25.2% prediction includes equality, so exactly 25.2% would meet that numerical ceiling. But the present plan contains no such observation. It would be premature to discuss that value as a measured outcome.
What would be an especially misleading way to combine the measurement and alignment steps in one sentence?

Saying “After confirming class-conditional feature shift, align the subset logits to correct it” would assume both that the shift has been confirmed and that alignment corrects it. The plan states neither. It calls for measuring the shift and aligning paired subset logits to a frozen full-input teacher, followed by evaluation.
Can you give a concise restatement that keeps those steps and both evaluation conditions?
Measure class-conditional feature shift; align paired subset logits to a frozen full-input teacher; then evaluate performance under reversals and measure complete-input accuracy.
So we should leave open whether the feature shift exists, whether alignment helps, and what happens to full-input accuracy?

Yes. The plan specifies how to investigate those questions and what to evaluate. It does not provide a class-conditional shift measurement, demonstrate an effect of alignment on reversal errors, or report complete-input accuracy.

For the CMU-MOSEI activity, I want to quantify class-conditional feature shift and compare group-DRO with paired-subset frozen-teacher alignment on three reversals and full-input accuracy. Can you unpack exactly what this covers?

It covers a measurement and a method comparison. On CMU-MOSEI, quantify feature shift within classes, then compare group-DRO with paired-subset alignment to a frozen full-input teacher. The comparison covers performance on three reversals and accuracy when the full input is available. The activity does not provide a shift value or any performance results.
What is the point of specifying class-conditional feature shift rather than feature shift in general?

Conditioning on class asks whether feature distributions differ among examples with the same label. An overall feature difference could instead reflect a different mix of labels. The class-conditional measurement addresses the narrower question, although the activity does not specify which features or distribution-comparison measure to use.
Does the activity assert that such a shift exists?
No. “Quantify” calls for measuring it; it does not supply a magnitude or even establish that a detectable shift will be found. Nor does it establish that any measured shift causes prediction error.
Could I use the reversal errors themselves as the measure of feature shift?

That would conflate two quantities. Reversal error measures predictive performance; class-conditional feature shift concerns differences in feature distributions within labels. The activity calls for the shift to be quantified and for performance to be compared, without treating one as a numerical substitute for the other.
When you say “within classes,” are you claiming that the same missingness pattern is held fixed?

No such conditioning rule is specified. It is important to distinguish a change in the mix of available subsets within a class from a change in the values of features that remain observed, but the activity does not prescribe the exact comparisons used to quantify shift. We should not present a particular conditioning scheme as already chosen.
What would it mean to compare group-DRO with paired-subset frozen-teacher alignment?

It means evaluating the two named approaches against one another under the stated conditions, rather than reporting alignment performance in isolation. The activity identifies group-DRO and paired-subset alignment to a frozen full-input teacher, but it does not specify architectures, training schedules, or a numerical advantage for either approach.
Should I call group-DRO the baseline in this comparison?

You can identify it as the comparison method. The activity says to compare group-DRO with the alignment approach; it does not itself assign a performance value or state which will do better. Calling it a comparison method avoids implying a result.
What is being paired in “paired-subset frozen-teacher alignment”?

The alignment plan concerns logits from subset inputs paired with corresponding outputs from a frozen full-input teacher. Pairing matters because the scores are to be related for corresponding prediction situations, not compared as unrelated collections. The activity does not specify which subsets are paired or how the pairs are constructed.
Does the frozen full-input teacher itself get updated as part of that alignment?

“Frozen” indicates that the teacher remains fixed during alignment. It serves as a full-input reference for the subset outputs. The activity does not say how the teacher was trained, what accuracy it achieves, or which other components are updated.
Is the comparison really between group-DRO and the teacher?

No. The named comparison is between group-DRO and the paired-subset alignment approach. The frozen full-input teacher is part of the alignment approach, providing the reference for alignment; the activity does not frame the teacher alone as the competing method.
Could I say the aligned subset predictor receives the full input at prediction time?

That would not follow from the activity. A full-input teacher is used as an alignment reference, while subset prediction concerns available subsets. Nothing here says the full input or the teacher’s output is available when a subset-based prediction is made.
Does alignment require the subset logits to match the teacher’s logits exactly?

No exact-match condition is specified. The activity names paired-subset frozen-teacher alignment but does not define an alignment loss, tolerance, or requirement for identical outputs. Those would be additional implementation details.
Why test three reversals rather than describe a single reversal result?

The activity explicitly requires a comparison on three reversals. Preserving that count matters: a result on only one would not describe the full set of conditions named here. The activity does not define the three reversals or provide their individual outcomes.
Does it tell us whether to average the errors across those three reversals?

No aggregation rule is given. The activity calls for comparing the approaches on three reversals; it does not say whether results should be reported individually, combined, or both. An average alone also would not reveal how either approach performed on each named condition.
Can I infer which reversal is hardest for either method?

No. The activity gives neither reversal-specific errors nor a ranking. The hardest reversal for one approach also need not be assumed to be the hardest for the other; determining that would require results not supplied here.
What measure is explicitly specified for the full-input part?

Full-input accuracy. It asks how the approaches perform when the complete input is available, separately from performance under reversal. The activity does not state an accuracy value or define which prediction route supplies the full-input output for either approach.
Does freezing the teacher mean full-input accuracy cannot change?

Not as a conclusion from this activity. Freezing describes the teacher during alignment; it does not fully specify how full-input predictions are produced or evaluated for the compared approaches. Full-input accuracy remains something to measure, not something guaranteed by that choice.
Should the full-input accuracy comparison be replaced by the teacher’s own accuracy?

No. The activity calls for comparing full-input accuracy alongside reversal performance. It does not say that the teacher’s accuracy is the reported full-input accuracy for the alignment approach, or that measuring the teacher alone would fulfill the comparison.
Are the shift measurement and the group-DRO-versus-alignment comparison meant to establish the same fact?

They address related but distinct questions. Quantifying class-conditional feature shift describes whether and how features differ within labels. Comparing the approaches tests their predictive performance under three reversals and with full input. A shift measurement alone does not determine which approach performs better, and a performance difference alone does not prove what caused the shift.
If alignment had lower reversal error than group-DRO, would that prove modality-feature selection was the cause?

No. If observed, it would establish a performance difference under the tested conditions. It would not uniquely identify the cause of the error or show that alignment specifically corrected within-class modality-feature selection. The causal explanation requires care even when the method comparison is clear.
And if we quantified a class-conditional shift, could we assume alignment would handle it?

No. Measuring a shift and successfully addressing it are separate matters. The activity includes the comparison precisely because the performance of group-DRO and paired-subset frozen-teacher alignment on the three reversals remains to be evaluated.
Can this activity, by itself, establish a worst-pattern error threshold for alignment?

Not without results. It specifies a comparison on three reversals, but reports no worst-pattern errors or threshold determination. The proposed ≤25.2% worst-pattern error ceiling is a hypothesis about alignment, not a finding contained in this activity.
What should I avoid implying about CMU-MOSEI here?

CMU-MOSEI is the named setting for the measurement and comparison. The activity does not say which modalities exhibit a feature shift, how large any shift is, or how its three reversals are constructed. Those particulars should not be supplied as facts.
Could you give a compact statement that preserves all the activity’s parts?
On CMU-MOSEI, quantify class-conditional feature shift, then compare group-DRO with paired-subset alignment to a frozen full-input teacher on three reversals and on full-input accuracy.
So at this point, neither the feature-shift magnitude nor the relative performance of the two approaches is specified?

Correct. The activity identifies what to measure and which approaches and conditions to compare. It leaves the class-conditional shift measurements, results on each of the three reversals, and full-input accuracy comparison open.
On CMU-MOSEI’s hardest reversal, within-class high-loss prevalence rose from 38% to 72%; teacher alignment yielded 26.4% error versus group-DRO’s 26.1%. How should I report this evidence?

Report the prevalence change and the method comparison separately: “On CMU-MOSEI’s hardest reversal, within-class high-loss prevalence rose from 38% to 72%. Teacher alignment yielded 26.4% error, compared with 26.1% for group-DRO.” Those figures describe this reversal; they do not provide results for the other reversals or for full-input accuracy.
How large is the change from 38% to 72%?
It is an increase of 34 percentage points: 72% minus 38%. Describing it as a 34% increase would confuse that direct difference with a relative change.
What does “within-class high-loss prevalence” tell us?

It concerns the proportion categorized as high-loss among examples considered within a class, rather than merely the overall frequency of different classes. The evidence gives the change from 38% to 72%, but does not identify particular classes, define the high-loss cutoff, or give separate prevalence values for each class.
Can I say the high-loss prevalence rose from 38% to 72% in every class?

No. “Within-class” identifies the kind of comparison, but the supplied figures do not establish that the same change occurred separately in every class. Keep the reported 38%-to-72% change without extending it to an unreported class-by-class breakdown.
Do we know exactly what the two prevalence percentages are measured against?

The evidence reports a rise from 38% to 72% on the hardest reversal, but does not spell out the two populations or conditions behind those endpoints. It would be premature to label either percentage as belonging to a particular training split, deployment population, or individual dropout pattern.
Is this prevalence change itself a measurement of modality-feature shift?

Not directly. It measures a change in the prevalence of high-loss examples within class. It does not report how the values of particular modality features changed or quantify a feature-distribution difference. Those are related questions, but the prevalence statistic should not be relabeled as a direct feature-shift measurement.
Does the rise show that difficult examples were selected under the reversal?

It shows that the reported high-loss prevalence rose substantially within class on the hardest reversal. That is consistent with a change in the mix of examples as characterized by loss, but the figures alone do not establish the selection mechanism or prove that it caused either predictor’s error.
Should I treat “high-loss” as an objective description of which examples are difficult?

It is safer to retain the measured term “high-loss.” The evidence does not define the loss threshold or establish a model-independent notion of difficulty. You can discuss why a changing high-loss prevalence is relevant to difficulty without treating that interpretation as an independently measured fact.
Turning to the predictors, what is the absolute error difference between 26.4% and 26.1%?
Teacher alignment’s reported error is 0.3 percentage points higher than group-DRO’s: 26.4% minus 26.1%. On this reversal and this reported measure, group-DRO has the lower error.
Would it be accurate to say group-DRO is 0.3% better?

“0.3 percentage points lower in error” is more precise. A 0.3% *relative* difference would use a denominator and mean something different. Also, “better” should be qualified to this error comparison on the hardest reversal, not extended to every condition.
Does 26.4% versus 26.1% establish which approach performs better across all three reversals?
No. Both reported errors concern the hardest CMU-MOSEI reversal. No paired errors for the other two reversals are supplied here, so the result does not establish an across-reversal ranking.
Can I call 26.4% the average error over the three reversals?
No. The 26.4% value is reported for teacher alignment on the hardest reversal. It is not stated to be an average over reversals. The same scope applies to the accompanying 26.1% group-DRO comparison.
Does “hardest reversal” tell us which missingness pattern caused the error?

No. It identifies the reversal as the hardest in the report, but does not identify an individual missingness pattern or explain how the reversal was designated hardest. Neither a pattern breakdown nor the other reversal errors are provided.
Can I refer to teacher alignment as paired-subset alignment to a frozen full-input teacher?

Yes; that identifies the alignment approach being compared with group-DRO. The observed result to attach to it is 26.4% error on the hardest reversal. The evidence does not say how closely the subset logits matched the teacher or give the teacher’s own accuracy.
Does the higher alignment error show that using a frozen teacher increased error?

It shows that teacher alignment’s reported error was 0.3 percentage points higher than group-DRO’s on this reversal. It does not isolate the effect of freezing the teacher or establish why the approaches differed. That causal interpretation would require information beyond these two errors.
Could both approaches be affected by the increase in high-loss prevalence?

That is possible, but these figures do not quantify how much the prevalence change affected either approach. The prevalence change and the two errors are reported for the same hardest-reversal context; their coexistence is not, by itself, a measured causal relationship.
Does the group-DRO comparison show that baseline-loss difficulty alone explains the error?

No. The 26.1% versus 26.4% comparison tells us which method had lower reported error on this reversal. The 38%-to-72% statistic tells us that high-loss prevalence changed within class. Neither observation by itself determines whether baseline-loss difficulty alone explains residual error or whether modality-feature selection also matters.
And does teacher alignment’s error rule out a within-class modality-feature effect?

No. Its 26.4% error is a performance observation, not a direct test that excludes such an effect. The evidence does not give a feature-specific shift measurement or a causal attribution of the remaining error.
Can I infer anything about accuracy with every input available?

Not from this evidence. It supplies within-class high-loss prevalence and an error comparison on the hardest reversal, but no full-input accuracy for teacher alignment or group-DRO. Error under reversal should not be substituted for complete-input accuracy.
What if I want to express the finding without speculating about its cause?

You could write: “On CMU-MOSEI’s hardest reversal, within-class high-loss prevalence rose by 34 percentage points, from 38% to 72%. Teacher alignment recorded 26.4% error, 0.3 percentage points higher than group-DRO’s 26.1%.” That states the observed changes and comparison without assigning a mechanism.
What is the main limit of that statement?

It is limited to the reported prevalence change and paired errors on the hardest reversal. It does not specify results on the other reversals, full-input accuracy, the size of any modality-feature shift, or why the error difference arose.

The decision is to defer teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO because both miss the 25.2% target, and instead investigate difficulty-aware calibration while retaining the full-input branch. Can you state that precisely?

Defer teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO as the approaches being pursued on their own: both miss the 25.2% error target. Investigate difficulty-aware calibration next, while retaining the full-input branch. This is a decision about what to investigate, not a claim that calibration will meet the target.
Does “defer” mean we have ruled out teacher alignment entirely?

No. Deferring teacher alignment means it is not the immediate focus of this decision. It does not say the approach is impossible, permanently rejected, or incapable of being useful in any other setting.
And why say “standalone group-DRO” rather than just “group-DRO”?

The qualification limits the decision to group-DRO pursued on its own. It does not state that every possible use of group-DRO, including a use alongside another approach, is excluded. No such combination is specified here, either.
What reason for deferring those approaches is actually stated?

The stated reason is that teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO both miss the 25.2% target. The decision does not assign a particular cause for either miss or claim that one approach fails for the same reason as the other.
Should I say one missed by more than the other?
That comparison is not part of this decision. Its stated basis is simply that both miss the 25.2% target. You can explain the decision without adding a ranking or repeating earlier error figures.
Does missing the target mean the approaches have no value at all?

No. Missing this specified target supports the decision to defer them in the stated roles. It does not establish that either approach is useless, or make a claim about every possible measure or condition.
What is difficulty-aware calibration intended to address, at a conceptual level?

It is a direction for investigating whether calibration that takes example difficulty into account can address the remaining error. The decision does not define how difficulty is measured, what quantity is calibrated, or how the calibration is carried out. Its effectiveness is still an open question.
Can I describe difficulty-aware calibration as the chosen solution?
It is the chosen direction to investigate, not a demonstrated solution. Saying it already meets the 25.2% target would turn a prospective investigation into an unsupported result.
Does this decision say that difficulty alone explains the error?
No. Choosing to investigate difficulty-aware calibration does not establish a causal explanation. It identifies something worth examining while leaving open why the error remains above the target.
Is a particular definition of difficulty now fixed?
No. The decision does not specify a difficulty score, a cutoff between easy and hard examples, or a method for estimating difficulty. Those would be additional design details.
Could I assume calibration means a particular adjustment to model scores?

No particular adjustment is specified. “Calibration” names the direction of inquiry, while “difficulty-aware” qualifies what that inquiry should take into account. The decision does not give an equation, training procedure, or output rule.
What does retaining the full-input branch commit us to?

It commits to keeping the branch for the case in which the full input is available while the difficulty-aware calibration direction is investigated. The decision does not say to replace that branch with teacher alignment, standalone group-DRO, or the proposed calibration.
Does retaining the branch mean its accuracy has been verified against the complete-modality baseline?
No. Keeping the branch is a design decision, not an accuracy result. It does not establish that full-input accuracy is within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline.
Is the retained full-input branch the same thing as the frozen full-input teacher?

The decision names the full-input branch to retain and teacher alignment to defer. It does not equate the branch with the frozen teacher used as an alignment reference. Treating them as necessarily identical would add a relationship that is not stated.
If teacher alignment is deferred, is its full-input teacher also required to remain in use?

The decision does not require that. It explicitly retains the full-input branch, not a teacher-alignment procedure. It gives no further instructions about using a frozen teacher during the new investigation.
Does difficulty-aware calibration replace the subset experts?

No replacement is specified. The decision identifies an investigation and says to retain the full-input branch; it does not define how calibration would interact with subset experts or which components it would alter.
Could I say the next investigation combines calibration with group-DRO?

Not as a fact of this decision. Standalone group-DRO is deferred, and difficulty-aware calibration is to be investigated. A combination is neither selected nor ruled out here, so describing one as the decided method would go beyond the statement.
Does the 25.2% figure apply to full-input accuracy?

No. It is the error target that teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO both miss in this decision. Full-input accuracy is a separate measure; retaining the full-input branch should not be confused with meeting a 25.2% accuracy target.
Do we know from this decision whether calibration will be evaluated on every reversal?

The decision does not lay out an evaluation protocol for calibration. It says to investigate difficulty-aware calibration because the two named approaches miss the 25.2% target, while retaining the full-input branch. We should not add a specified number of reversals or an outcome to this decision.
Can I frame this as a rejection of all alignment methods?

No. The decision specifically defers teacher alignment. It does not make a blanket judgment about every form of alignment, just as deferring standalone group-DRO does not decide the status of every possible group-based method.
What should I avoid implying about the reason for the target misses?

Avoid assigning an unreported mechanism—for example, claiming the misses prove that difficulty, feature selection, or calibration is the decisive cause. The reason given for the decision is the narrower performance comparison: both named approaches miss the 25.2% target.
Is there any promise that difficulty-aware calibration will preserve full-input accuracy?
No. Retaining the full-input branch keeps that case represented, but the decision contains no measured accuracy and no guarantee about how an eventual calibration approach would affect it.
How can I distinguish the decision from the finding that motivated it?

The finding stated in the decision is that teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO both miss the 25.2% target. The decision is to defer them, investigate difficulty-aware calibration, and retain the full-input branch. The finding motivates the change in focus; it does not establish the outcome of the new investigation.
Would it be accurate to write, “Calibration fixes the remaining error, so teacher alignment and group-DRO are abandoned”?

No. That wording asserts an unmeasured benefit, drops the important “standalone” qualification on group-DRO, and turns “defer” into “abandon.” The stated decision is more limited: investigate difficulty-aware calibration while retaining the full-input branch, because teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO both miss the 25.2% target.
Give me a concise version suitable for recording the decision.
Defer teacher alignment and standalone group-DRO because both miss the 25.2% target; investigate difficulty-aware calibration while retaining the full-input branch.
And that leaves the calibration outcome open?
Yes. The decision changes what is being investigated. It does not report that difficulty-aware calibration has reduced error, met the 25.2% target, or preserved full-input accuracy.

I propose training difficulty-stratified, minimax-calibrated gating over unimodal and subset experts, while retaining an isolated full-input branch for complete cases. Can you unpack that as a proposal rather than a result?

The proposal introduces a gate that makes use of unimodal and subset experts, with its training organized by difficulty strata and a minimax-calibrated objective. It also keeps an isolated full-input branch for cases where all inputs are present. This specifies a direction for the predictor’s design; it does not report that the gate has been trained or that either missingness robustness or complete-input accuracy has improved.
What is the gate meant to do at a conceptual level?

A gate determines how to draw on the available experts for a prediction. Here, those experts include unimodal experts and subset experts. The proposal does not say whether the gate chooses a single expert, combines their outputs, or uses some other rule, so the precise form of that decision remains open.
Why name both unimodal and subset experts?

They are distinct kinds of candidate predictors: a unimodal expert uses one modality, while a subset expert is intended to use an available subset. The proposal calls for gating over both kinds rather than specifying that only one kind supplies predictions under missingness. It does not identify the modalities, subsets, or number of experts.
Does gating over a unimodal expert mean the final predictor is simply unimodal?

No. Unimodal experts are among the candidates the gate can draw on; subset experts are also included. The proposal does not prescribe which candidate will be used in any particular case, or how much influence each will have.
How should I read “difficulty-stratified” without inventing a difficulty score?

It means difficulty distinctions are to be represented in the gate’s training rather than treating all cases as a single undifferentiated collection. The proposal does not specify how difficulty is measured, where stratum boundaries lie, or how many strata there are. In particular, it should not be paraphrased as though one particular measure of difficulty has already been selected.
Is difficulty stratification the same thing as separating examples by label?

Not necessarily. Difficulty and label describe different distinctions. The proposal specifically calls the gating difficulty-stratified; it does not define its strata as labels or prescribe a joint label-and-difficulty grouping.
Could I say each difficulty stratum gets its own gate?

That would be one possible implementation, but it is not specified. “Difficulty-stratified gating” indicates that the training accounts for difficulty strata; it does not say whether there is one gate per stratum, a single gate informed by strata, or another arrangement.
What does “minimax” contribute?

At a high level, minimax directs attention to poor performance in the worst relevant condition rather than optimizing only a favorable average. That is consistent with caring about worst-pattern error under missingness. The proposal does not define the precise conditions over which a maximum is taken or supply a mathematical objective.
Does minimax mean the gate is guaranteed to work on an unseen missingness shift?

No. It describes an intended training emphasis, not a guarantee of performance outside the conditions actually evaluated. The proposal does not establish that the gate will handle every unseen label-dependent missingness shift.
And how should I explain the “calibrated” part?

It qualifies the gating approach: the gate is intended to be calibrated while making use of the experts under the minimax emphasis. The proposal does not define a calibration criterion, specify what quantity is calibrated, or claim a measured calibration result. It would be too specific to supply a particular calibration formula as though one were already chosen.
Is “minimax-calibrated” one claim or two finished accomplishments?

Neither is a finished accomplishment here. Together, the words characterize the proposed training of the gate. They do not report that a minimax objective has been optimized successfully or that calibration has been verified.
What does the isolated full-input branch do in this design?

It preserves a distinct path for complete cases, when all inputs are present, rather than making that case depend solely on the proposed gate over unimodal and subset experts. The proposal says to retain that branch; it does not provide its measured accuracy or define all of its internal details.
Does “isolated” mean I can say exactly how the branch is trained or connected to the experts?

No. It conveys separation of the full-input branch from the proposed gating path, but the proposal does not spell out parameter sharing, a supervision rule, or an implementation boundary. Those details should not be filled in as established design choices.
Should I claim that complete cases definitely bypass the gate?

The proposal specifically retains an isolated full-input branch for complete cases, so it is fair to identify that branch as their intended path. It does not, however, specify an exact routing algorithm or every possible interaction between that branch and the gate. Avoid turning the broad design distinction into an unstated implementation rule.
Why keep complete cases distinct from missing-input cases?

They place different demands on the predictor. The gate over unimodal and subset experts is proposed to address varying available inputs, while the isolated branch keeps the complete-input case explicitly represented. Keeping it distinct is intended to avoid sacrificing performance when all inputs are present, but that intended protection still needs to be assessed.
Does this proposal promise the goal’s 10% relative worst-pattern error reduction against the strongest unimodal baseline?

No. That reduction is a performance requirement for the goal, not an outcome established by proposing a difficulty-stratified, minimax-calibrated gate. Including unimodal experts in the gate also does not, by itself, establish a relative improvement over the strongest unimodal baseline.
What about keeping complete-modality accuracy within one percentage point of an equally trained complete-modality baseline?

Retaining an isolated full-input branch addresses that concern in the proposed design, but does not establish the one-percentage-point accuracy condition. The branch’s complete-input accuracy still has to be distinguished from the comparator’s accuracy; neither value is given in this proposal.
Is the gate necessarily allowed to use the missingness mask as a label cue?

The proposal does not specify what inputs the gate receives or whether a mask is represented explicitly. A gate must somehow operate in situations with different available inputs, but that does not settle whether it uses availability only to choose usable experts or also exploits a mask–label association. No rule resolving that question is stated here.
Can I say difficulty-stratified gating fixes within-class selection?

Not as an established fact. Difficulty stratification is part of the proposed approach, but the proposal neither proves a particular selection mechanism nor shows that the gate corrects it. Its effect on error remains open.
Would it be accurate to describe minimax calibration as selecting the most reliable expert for every individual example?

That is more specific than the proposal. It names a minimax-calibrated gate over experts, but does not define reliability at the example level or guarantee selection of the best expert for each case. The gate’s decision rule and performance have not been specified.
Does the proposal tell us whether the unimodal and subset experts are retrained along with the gate?

No. It calls for training the difficulty-stratified, minimax-calibrated gating over those experts, without saying whether the experts themselves are fixed, jointly updated, or trained in another way during that process.
Can you give me a compact formulation that retains every part of the proposed design?
Train a difficulty-stratified, minimax-calibrated gate over unimodal and subset experts, while retaining an isolated full-input branch for complete cases.
And what should remain open when I present it?

The precise difficulty strata, gating and calibration rules, and training details remain unspecified, as do the resulting worst-pattern error and complete-input accuracy. The sentence proposes a design; it does not assert that the robustness or accuracy requirements have been achieved.
Can expert disagreement identify hard incomplete cases without letting the gate exploit shifting mask–label correlations?

Possibly, but those are two separate questions. Disagreement among unimodal and subset experts could indicate that an incomplete case is difficult to predict. It could also reflect which experts are available under a particular missingness pattern. If that pattern is correlated with labels during training and the correlation shifts, a gate might learn a shortcut through disagreement even without receiving an explicit mask.
Why would disagreement signal difficulty at all?

When experts given the available information reach different predictions, their disagreement can indicate uncertainty or conflicting evidence. That makes it a plausible signal for a hard case. It is not a definition of difficulty, though: experts can agree and still be wrong, or disagree even when one has useful evidence.
So a high-disagreement case is not necessarily a high-error case?

Correct. Disagreement describes how the experts’ outputs relate to one another. Error describes how predictions relate to the true label. The question is whether the first can help identify difficult incomplete cases without becoming an unreliable cue about the second.
What makes an incomplete case different for this purpose?

With incomplete inputs, the available experts may have access to different amounts or kinds of information. Their disagreement could arise from genuine ambiguity in what remains observed, from differing expert behavior, or from the availability pattern itself. The question does not specify which explanation applies.
If the gate never receives the missingness mask explicitly, is the shortcut risk gone?

Not necessarily. The collection of expert outputs—or even which outputs exist—may reveal something about which modalities are available. If the gate can infer availability from those signals, it might still exploit a training-time mask–label correlation that later shifts. Excluding an explicit mask input would not, on its own, establish that the gate is independent of the mask.
Could the amount of disagreement itself act as a proxy for the mask?

Yes, in principle. If some availability patterns tend to produce more disagreement than others, a disagreement measure might carry information about the pattern. Whether that happens for the proposed experts is open; the conceptual risk is that the gate could mistake a pattern-linked signal for a stable indication of label or difficulty.
Does that mean the gate should ignore disagreement?

The question does not require that conclusion. Disagreement may still contain useful information about a case. The issue is whether the gate can use it to assess prediction difficulty without depending on an incidental association between missingness patterns and labels. No rule for accomplishing that separation is specified here.
Can you distinguish a legitimate use of availability from an illegitimate shortcut?

Availability legitimately tells the gate which expert outputs can be used and what information those experts had. The shortcut concern arises if the gate treats the availability pattern, or a proxy for it, as evidence that a particular label is more likely solely because that association held in training. When the association shifts, that label cue may become misleading.
Would disagreement between a unimodal expert and a subset expert be more informative than disagreement between two unimodal experts?

The question does not establish a ranking. Different experts can disagree for different reasons, including differences in the information they receive. Without specifying the experts and the incomplete cases, we cannot assume that one pairing supplies a more reliable difficulty signal than another.
What if the gate sees only the final predictions from the experts?

Even final predictions can exhibit patterns associated with availability. Limiting what the gate sees might change what it can infer, but it would not automatically establish that disagreement reflects difficulty rather than the missingness pattern. The question leaves the gate’s inputs unspecified.
Would giving the gate expert confidence scores resolve the ambiguity?

Not automatically. Confidence scores might help characterize how strongly experts favor their predictions, but their behavior could also vary across available subsets. Adding them would be a design choice not stated in the question, and their presence would not guarantee protection against a shifting mask–label correlation.
Is there a way to express what we want from disagreement without choosing an implementation?

Conceptually, we want disagreement to indicate difficulty arising from the evidence available for a particular case, not to stand in for a training-time association between its missingness mask and its label. That describes the desired distinction, not a proven property of the gate or a specified method for enforcing it.
Does low disagreement mean the gate can safely trust the experts?
No. Experts can make the same mistake. Low disagreement says their outputs are similar; it does not establish that their shared prediction is correct or robust when mask–label relationships change.
Could disagreement also be high merely because the experts use different subsets?

Yes. Experts with different available inputs may produce different outputs because those inputs provide different evidence. That difference could be relevant to uncertainty, but it need not mean the particular case is intrinsically difficult. It could instead be tied to what information was withheld.
When mask–label correlations shift, what exactly could go wrong with the gate?

A gate might learn that a particular configuration of available experts or their disagreement usually accompanies one label in training. If that association changes, the same gate behavior could favor an inappropriate prediction. The concern is about dependence on an unstable correlation, not a claim that the proposed gate has already learned one.
Does the minimax-calibrated aspect of the gating proposal guarantee protection?

No. It characterizes the proposed gate, but neither the calibration criterion nor the conditions covered by the minimax emphasis are specified here. Those words alone do not establish that disagreement will be a valid difficulty signal under shifting mask–label correlations.
Could difficulty stratification distinguish hard cases from mask patterns?

It might be intended to help with that distinction, but the question remains open. If a difficulty signal tracks availability rather than case difficulty, stratifying on it might preserve the very shortcut of concern. The proposal does not define the strata or demonstrate what they capture.
Is the problem that masks should never influence which expert the gate can use?

No. A gate cannot use an expert’s output if that output is unavailable, so availability has an operational role. The risk is using availability, directly or through expert disagreement, as a label cue whose correlation with the label can shift.
Could we assess disagreement among experts that are available for the same missingness pattern?

That is a useful conceptual distinction: considering disagreement under a fixed availability pattern would reduce confusion between changes in the set of available experts and differences among cases with that pattern. It would not by itself prove that disagreement identifies difficulty, and the question does not prescribe a particular assessment procedure.
Why would fixing the pattern not completely solve it?

Because disagreement within a pattern can still reflect differences in expert behavior rather than reliable differences in case difficulty. Also, a gate must operate across incomplete cases, potentially with different patterns. Understanding disagreement within one pattern does not automatically show how its meaning transfers across patterns or under a shifted mask–label relationship.
If disagreement predicts errors during training, isn't that enough?

Not for the concern stated here. A training-time association could partly arise from the prevailing relationship between masks and labels. The question asks whether disagreement remains useful for identifying hard incomplete cases when that relationship shifts, without the gate exploiting the relationship itself.
Does the isolated full-input branch answer the question for incomplete cases?

No. The isolated full-input branch serves complete cases. The question is specifically about a gate using disagreement among experts for incomplete cases while mask–label correlations may shift. Keeping the full-input branch distinct does not, by itself, establish how that gate behaves.
Can we conclude that expert disagreement will fail as a difficulty signal?

No. There are plausible reasons it could be informative and plausible ways it could be misleading. The question identifies the distinction that matters, but gives no measurement of disagreement, gate behavior, or performance under shifted correlations.
What would be too strong a claim in the other direction?

Saying that expert disagreement reliably identifies every hard incomplete case, or that using it makes the gate immune to shifting mask–label correlations, would be too strong. Neither follows from the fact that the experts sometimes disagree.
How would you summarize the uncertainty in one sentence?

Expert disagreement may help identify difficult incomplete cases, but it may also encode availability patterns, so it remains open whether a gate can use it without exploiting mask–label correlations that shift.
And the distinction to preserve is disagreement as evidence about a case versus disagreement as a proxy for its mask?

Exactly. The open question is whether the gate can draw on disagreement that reflects difficulty in the available evidence while avoiding dependence on disagreement that merely tracks an unstable relationship between the missingness mask and the label.

My hypothesis is that mask-blind, disagreement-calibrated minimax gating will reduce hardest-reversal error below 25.2% while preserving full-input accuracy above 81.2%. Can you state it without making it sound like a result?

We hypothesize that mask-blind, disagreement-calibrated minimax gating will achieve error below 25.2% on the hardest reversal while retaining full-input accuracy above 81.2%. Both are predicted outcomes, not measured results.
What is the role of disagreement in this hypothesis?

Disagreement among the experts is proposed as a signal the gate can use when handling incomplete cases. Calling the gate “disagreement-calibrated” suggests that its use of that signal should be calibrated, rather than assuming disagreement always identifies a hard case. The hypothesis does not specify a disagreement measure or a calibration procedure.
Does it claim that disagreement reliably identifies difficulty?

No. The hypothesis predicts performance from the proposed gating approach. It does not establish that disagreement is a reliable difficulty measure in every case or that any particular disagreement value corresponds to a particular error risk.
How does “mask-blind” fit with a gate that has to handle incomplete inputs?

Mask-blindness expresses the intended restriction against supplying the missingness mask as an explicit label cue. It does not imply that the gate can use an unavailable expert output, or that the outputs it receives reveal nothing about availability. The hypothesis does not specify exactly how the restriction is implemented.
Could the gate still infer the missingness pattern from which experts respond?

Possibly. Which expert outputs are available may convey information about the available inputs. That is why mask-blindness alone should not be described as proof that the gate cannot pick up a mask-related shortcut. The hypothesis predicts an outcome despite that concern; it does not settle the gate’s internal behavior.
Could disagreement itself reveal the pattern indirectly?

Yes, in principle. If disagreement varies with which experts can make predictions, it could act as a proxy for availability. The open issue is whether the gate uses disagreement in a way that helps with difficult cases without depending on a mask–label association that may shift. No such separation is demonstrated by the hypothesis alone.
What does minimax add to the prediction?

It indicates an intended emphasis on poor-performing conditions rather than only on average performance. That is pertinent to the prediction about error on the hardest reversal. The hypothesis does not define the minimax objective or identify the conditions included in it, so the word does not guarantee the predicted error.
Are mask-blindness, disagreement calibration, and minimax gating separate claims of success?

They are qualifications of the proposed gating approach. The performance claims are the two thresholds: hardest-reversal error below 25.2% and full-input accuracy above 81.2%. Merely describing the gate with those qualifications does not establish either outcome.
What exactly does “hardest-reversal error” refer to?

It refers to error on the reversal regarded as hardest in the relevant evaluation. The hypothesis sets a threshold for that error; it does not identify the reversal, explain how it is designated hardest, or provide errors for other reversal conditions.
Should I automatically call that value worst-pattern error?

This hypothesis says “hardest-reversal error.” Worst-pattern error has been an important measure in the broader discussion, but the hypothesis does not explicitly state how error is summarized within the hardest reversal. Keep its wording unless that measure is specified separately.
Is the hardest-reversal threshold inclusive?
No. “Below 25.2%” is strict: error must be less than 25.2%. An error of exactly 25.2% would not meet this prediction.
And how strict is “above 81.2%” for full-input accuracy?
It is strict as well. Full-input accuracy must exceed 81.2%; exactly 81.2% would not meet the prediction.
So one threshold is an upper bound on error and the other a lower bound on accuracy?

Yes. For the hardest reversal, lower error is the desired direction and the predicted value is strictly below 25.2%. With full input, higher accuracy is the desired direction and the predicted value is strictly above 81.2%. Both conditions are part of the same hypothesis.
Does “preserving” full-input accuracy mean the accuracy must be unchanged?

Not in this statement. Its explicit numerical prediction is accuracy above 81.2% when the full input is available. It does not say accuracy must be identical to another value, nor does it give a new percentage-point comparison with a baseline.
Is 81.2% the accuracy of a baseline?
The hypothesis presents 81.2% as a threshold for full-input accuracy. It does not identify that number as a measured baseline accuracy or specify a comparator from which it was derived.
Likewise, is 25.2% a unimodal error in this hypothesis?

No such identification is made. Here 25.2% is the strict ceiling predicted for hardest-reversal error. The hypothesis does not state a new error value for a unimodal comparator or express its prediction as a relative reduction against one.
Could someone meet the hypothesis with good full-input accuracy but error of exactly 25.2% on the hardest reversal?
No. Even if full-input accuracy exceeds 81.2%, an error of exactly 25.2% would fail the “below 25.2%” condition. Both thresholds must be met.
What if the reversal error is below 25.2% but full-input accuracy equals 81.2%?
That would also fail the stated prediction, because “above 81.2%” excludes equality. Improving one condition cannot substitute for meeting the other.
Does the hypothesis say the gate will select the correct expert for every incomplete case?

No. It predicts an error threshold under the hardest reversal, not perfect prediction or selection of the best expert for each individual case. It also does not specify whether the gate selects one expert or combines several.
Can I specify which expert disagreement statistic the gate uses?

Not as part of this hypothesis as written. It names disagreement-calibrated gating but gives no statistic, source of scores, or calibration rule. Adding one would turn a general hypothesis into a more specific design claim.
Does the hypothesis say that the full-input branch is replaced by the gate?

No. The proposed gating approach sits alongside an isolated full-input branch for complete cases. This hypothesis predicts full-input accuracy above 81.2%, but does not say to replace that branch or specify exactly how the complete-case output is produced.
Is it fair to say the two thresholds reflect the two situations the predictor must handle?

Yes. Hardest-reversal error concerns a challenging missing-input condition, while full-input accuracy concerns cases where all inputs are observed. The hypothesis asks the proposed gating approach to satisfy both conditions, without assuming that success on one establishes success on the other.
Would meeting both thresholds prove the gate never exploited a shifting mask–label correlation?

No. Meeting the thresholds would establish the specified performance outcomes under the evaluated conditions, not a complete account of what cues the gate used. The mask-shortcut concern motivates the mask-blind qualification, but predictive performance alone would not prove that every possible proxy for the mask was excluded.
Could failure to meet either threshold tell us which part of the gating approach was responsible?

Not by itself. A threshold miss would identify which performance prediction was not met. It would not isolate whether mask-blindness, disagreement calibration, the minimax emphasis, or some other aspect accounted for the outcome.
How can I avoid turning the hypothesis into a claim that the gate has already been trained and evaluated?

Lead with “we hypothesize” or “we predict,” and describe the two numbers as thresholds to be tested. Do not attach measured errors, accuracies, or causal explanations that are not supplied by this hypothesis.
Give me a concise version with both strict inequalities and the complete-case condition intact.
We hypothesize that mask-blind, disagreement-calibrated minimax gating will yield hardest-reversal error <25.2% while maintaining full-input accuracy >81.2% when all inputs are available.
And neither side of that sentence should be presented as already demonstrated?

Correct. It predicts both an error below 25.2% on the hardest reversal and accuracy above 81.2% with full input. The hypothesis supplies no measurements showing that either threshold has been reached.

Could the gate choose one expert, or could it combine several?

What does the minimax part mean without writing an objective that has not been chosen?

Does minimax training itself guarantee low worst-pattern error under reversal?

What is a reversal in the evaluation?

Can I say the activity tests three reversals because earlier work considered three?

The CMU-MOSEI results are in: across three reversals, gating yielded 24.9% worst-pattern error versus 28.0% for the unimodal comparator; full-input accuracy was 81.6% versus 82.2%. How should I report them?

The gate’s reported error is 3.1 percentage points lower: 28.0% minus 24.9%. Both percentages are errors, so the lower value is the favorable direction for this comparison.
And what is the relative reduction against 28.0%?

Using the unimodal error as the denominator, (28.0 − 24.9) ÷ 28.0 is approximately 0.1107. That is about an 11.1% relative reduction in the reported worst-pattern error. The absolute difference is still 3.1 percentage points.
So I should not say the error fell by 11.1 percentage points?
Correct. It fell by 3.1 percentage points, from 28.0% to 24.9%. The approximately 11.1% figure describes that difference relative to the 28.0% comparator, not a percentage-point subtraction.

It preserves the scope of the reported evaluation: three CMU-MOSEI reversal conditions were considered. The evidence gives one reported worst-pattern error comparison across that evaluation. It does not provide a separate error for each reversal or state exactly how results from the three conditions were summarized.
Can I say the gate achieved 24.9% on each of the three reversals?
No. A single reported value across three reversals does not imply the same value on each one. The individual reversal errors are not supplied.

No averaging rule is stated. It is reported as worst-pattern error across three reversals. Calling it a mean of three reversal-specific values would add an interpretation that the evidence does not specify.
